en.title: Urban and Regional Planning: the whole course
en.short: What urban and regional planning covers, how planning degrees are organised, and how to study them well.

sections.heading: What urban and regional planning is
sections.text:
Urban and regional planning is the study and practice of guiding how land, buildings, transport, services and natural resources are used. Planners prepare plans and policies for neighbourhoods, towns, cities and regions, and they also control new development through permits and conditions. The work sits between design, law, economics and public policy, so planners must argue with numbers and with people.

The subject matters because land is scarce and shared. A road, a market or a housing estate built in the wrong place can waste public money for decades and push poorer households out of reach of work. Planning tries to see these effects before they happen.

These summaries teach principles and methods. They do not replace the planning law, development control rules or professional registration of any country. Those differ, and they change. Check the current official source, and check your own department’s handbook.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
Nigerian universities usually offer urban and regional planning as a four or five year bachelor’s degree, often with a period of supervised practical training, and polytechnics offer an ND and then an HND. In the UK, planning degrees are often accredited by the Royal Town Planning Institute, and some students take a three year bachelor’s followed by a master’s. Ghana, Kenya, South Africa and other countries each have their own patterns. Lengths, awards and accreditation differ, so read your own handbook rather than trusting a general rule.

The early years are usually shared: introduction to planning, history, urban geography, statistics, mapping and GIS, economics and sociology. The middle years move to land use, housing, transport, infrastructure, environment and law. Later years add studio work, a comprehensive plan project, professional practice and, at master’s level, theory, resilience, smart cities and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The course opens with foundations. Introduction to planning explains what planners do. History shows how ideas such as the garden city and colonial town layouts shaped African cities. Urban geography and settlement systems explain why towns grow where they do. Planning statistics and mathematics give the tools for analysing population, land and demand. Maps, cartography and GIS teach you to read and make spatial information. Urban economics and urban sociology explain land values, markets, communities and inequality. Environmental systems cover water, soil, air and ecology. Site planning and graphics teach drawing and site analysis, and urban form and land use patterns show how cities are laid out.

The core then turns to practice: planning theory and the public interest, land use planning and zoning, urban design and placemaking, housing, transport, infrastructure, regional development, environmental impact assessment, planning law and development control, land administration, community participation, GIS analysis, project appraisal and the studio comprehensive plan. Professional practice covers ethics and registration, such as TOPREC in Nigeria. Master’s topics are advanced theory, resilience and climate, smart cities and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read each topic with a place in mind. Choose a town you know, such as where you grew up, and ask how its layout, transport and housing came to be. Sketch maps from memory, then check them against a real map. That habit builds spatial thinking faster than reading alone.

Practise the quantitative parts: population projections, densities, land budgets and simple project appraisal. Show your units and check whether the answer is plausible.

For law and policy, learn the principle and the purpose, then find the current statute or code for your country. Do not memorise clause numbers from an old handout.

Take studio work seriously. It is where the separate subjects come together.

sections.heading: Common mistakes

keyPoints: Urban and regional planning guides how land, buildings, transport and services are used, from neighbourhood to region.
Planning degrees differ in length, award and accreditation by country, so check your own handbook.
These summaries teach principles and methods and do not replace your country’s planning law or registration rules.
Study each topic against a real town you know, and sketch maps to build spatial thinking.

Plans must propose and justify with evidence, not merely describe what exists.

en.title: Introduction to Urban and Regional Planning
en.short: Definitions, scope, planning scales and how planners differ from architects, engineers and geographers.

sections.heading: Definition and scope
sections.text:
Urban and regional planning is the organised process of guiding future development of settlements and regions. It aims to improve living conditions and balance social, economic and environmental needs. Planners study land use, movement, housing, services and the environment, and propose policies, plans and controls. Its scope runs from a neighbourhood to a region. Planning is spatial and future-oriented: it asks where activities should go and how they connect. It serves the public interest.

Planning uses evidence, consultation and law. A plan may set goals, allocate land, coordinate public investment and regulate private development. Registration differs by country. In Nigeria, town planners are registered by the Town Planners Registration Council of Nigeria (TOPREC); engineers are regulated by COREN.

sections.heading: Scales of planning
sections.text:
Planning scales are levels of area and detail. Neighbourhood planning covers a few streets: schools, open space, local shops and safe walking. City or municipal planning covers the whole town: land-use zones, transport networks, water and waste services, and growth areas. Regional planning covers several cities and their rural surroundings: city-region links, corridors and uneven development.

Example: in the made-up Kowa district, 20,000 people need a health centre. A neighbourhood plan checks walking distance and plot size. A city plan checks roads and budget. A regional plan checks whether nearby towns also need services, so money is not wasted.

sections.heading: Roles and related fields
sections.text:
Planners act as analysts, policy advisers, facilitators, regulators and project managers. They gather evidence, compare options and coordinate agencies. A planner may write a local plan, assess a development application or manage a regeneration project.

Planning differs from architecture, engineering and geography. Architecture designs buildings and their setting. Engineering designs and builds infrastructure. Geography studies spatial patterns and processes to explain them. Planning is normative and interventionist: it uses such knowledge to decide what should happen and coordinate action. In Kowa, an architect designs the clinic, an engineer its drainage, a geographer maps travel flows, and the planner compares sites and leads consultation.

keyPoints: Urban and regional planning guides future settlement and regional development to meet social, economic and environmental goals.
Planning scales run from neighbourhood to city and region, with more detail at smaller scales and broader coordination at larger scales.
Planners act as analysts, advisers, facilitators, regulators and project managers, not only as map-makers.
Architecture designs buildings, engineering designs infrastructure, and geography explains spatial patterns; planning uses such knowledge to decide and coordinate action.
Professional registration and planning law differ by country; in Nigeria town planners register with TOPREC, while engineers are regulated by COREN.
Plans combine evidence, consultation and legal controls to serve the public interest.

en.title: History of Urban and Regional Planning
en.short: From ancient cities to industrialisation, garden cities, modernism, regional planning and African colonial legacies.

sections.heading: Ancient and pre-colonial
sections.text: Urban planning is the deliberate shaping of settlements: streets, plots, services and public spaces. Ancient cities in Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, Egypt, Greece and Rome used grids, walls, drains and monuments. Pre-colonial African cities also showed planning: Benin City had long walls and straight streets; Timbuktu and Great Zimbabwe had organised layouts; many Yoruba towns had walls, markets and compounds. Rulers and customs guided building, not a professional planning system. Planning was often religious or defensive, and it served rulers, with little public participation.

sections.heading: Industry and reform
sections.text: Industrial urbanisation in Europe from the late eighteenth century packed workers into unhealthy housing. Public health reforms brought sewers, water and building rules. Ebenezer Howard’s garden city idea (1898) proposed self-contained towns of limited size, surrounded by farmland, to combine town and country. Letchworth (1903) was the first. Modernist planning, linked to Le Corbusier and the CIAM group of architects, favoured tall blocks, separated functions and car-based circulation. The garden city movement influenced new towns and suburbs in many countries. These ideas spread worldwide.

sections.heading: Regions, colonies, independence
sections.text: In the 1940s, regional planning treated the city and its hinterland together. Patrick Abercrombie’s Greater London Plan (1944) proposed new towns and green belts. In colonial Africa, planning often used master plans (long-term layout plans) and zoning (land-use rules) to separate European and African areas. Colonial planning also laid railways, ports and administrative quarters for export economies. After independence, post-colonial governments inherited these laws and agencies. A concrete case: Nairobi’s colonial plans reserved separate zones; post-independence plans tried to integrate the city but faced rapid growth and informal settlements.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Old ideas still shape practice: garden-city green belts, modernist zoning, regional agencies and colonial legal frameworks. Knowing their origins helps planners judge what to keep, adapt or replace. Historical ideas are not neutral: they carry assumptions about order, health and who belongs where. Planning law and professional registration differ by country, so check current official sources.

keyPoints: Urban planning is the deliberate shaping of settlements; ancient and pre-colonial cities used grids, walls, drains and organised layouts.
Industrial urbanisation caused overcrowding and disease, leading to public health reforms and building rules.
Ebenezer Howard’s garden city idea (1898) proposed limited-size towns surrounded by farmland; Letchworth (1903) was the first.
Modernist planning, linked to Le Corbusier and CIAM, favoured tall blocks, separated functions and car-based circulation.
Regional planning from the 1940s treated the city and its hinterland together, as in Patrick Abercrombie’s Greater London Plan (1944).
Colonial planning in Africa often used master plans and segregation; post-independence states inherited these systems, which still shape practice.

en.title: Urban Geography and Settlement Systems
en.short: Urbanisation, settlement hierarchies, central place theory, rural-urban links and regional patterns.

sections.heading: Urbanisation and hierarchy
sections.text:
Urbanisation is the rising share of a population living in urban areas. Urban growth is the absolute rise in urban numbers, so a country can have urban growth without urbanisation. What counts as "urban" is set by each country’s statistical authority, so figures are not strictly comparable across countries.

Settlements form a hierarchy: hamlet, village, town, city, metropolis, conurbation (a cluster of towns and cities that have grown together). Higher levels hold more people and more specialised services. The United Nations commonly uses "megacity" for an agglomeration above 10 million people.

sections.heading: Central place theory
sections.text:
Walter Christaller (1933) asked why towns of different sizes are spaced as they are. A central place sells goods to a surrounding region. Each good has a range, the farthest customers will travel, and a threshold, the least demand that keeps a supplier in business. Low-order goods such as bread have short ranges and appear in small towns; high-order goods such as specialist hospitals need large thresholds and appear in few large centres. Christaller’s hexagonal market areas assume a flat plain, evenly spread farm population and equal transport in all directions. Real terrain and roads distort the pattern, so treat it as a teaching model.

Example: a clinic needs 5,000 visits a year. Its catchment, the area it serves, holds 20,000 people making 0.4 visits each per year: 20,000 × 0.4 = 8,000 visits, so the threshold is met.

sections.heading: Rural-urban linkages
sections.text: Towns and their hinterlands, the rural areas around them, exchange people, food, cash, remittances and waste. Circular migration, where a worker moves to town for work but returns regularly to a rural home, is common in West Africa. Regional patterns include the primate city, one city far larger than the next, and the rank-size rule, where the nth city is about 1/n the size of the largest. The rule is a rough regularity, not a law.

sections.heading: Geography in planning
sections.text: Planners use this analysis to site schools and clinics, map service catchments, project population and identify growth corridors. A settlement hierarchy shows where investment serves most people for the least travel.

keyPoints: Urbanisation is a rising urban share; urban growth is a rising urban number.
"Urban" is defined nationally, so cross-country comparisons need care.
Central place theory links a good’s range and threshold to where it is supplied.
Rank-size rule: the nth city is roughly 1/n the size of the largest.
A catchment’s demand must exceed a facility’s threshold for it to be viable.
Settlement hierarchies guide where services are sited and how far people travel.

en.title: Planning Mathematics and Statistics
en.short: Summarising planning data: averages, rates, indices, population projection, sampling and probability.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise a dataset. The mean is the sum divided by the count. The median is the middle value once the data are sorted. The mode is the most frequent value. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. The standard deviation measures how far values spread around the mean.

Four ward populations, in thousands: 12, 15, 18, 15.
Mean = 60 ÷ 4 = 15. Median = 15. Mode = 15. Range = 18 − 12 = 6.
Deviations from 15 are −3, 0, 3, 0; their squares sum to 18.
Population standard deviation = √(18 ÷ 4) = 2.12 thousand.

sections.heading: Rates, ratios, indices
sections.text:
A rate relates a count to a population and a time period. Crude birth rate = births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000. With 3,600 births and 120,000 people: 3,600 ÷ 120,000 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000. A ratio compares two parts. Sex ratio = males ÷ females × 100; with 61,200 males and 58,800 females it is 104.1.

An index number shows change against a base year, which is set at 100. Index = current value ÷ base value × 100. A population of 80,000 in the base year and 96,000 later gives 96,000 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 120, a rise of 20 per cent.

sections.heading: Projection, sampling, probability
sections.text:
Population projection extends past growth forward. With a constant growth rate r, P = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ. From 100,000 at 2.5 per cent for 10 years: 100,000 × 1.025¹⁰ ≈ 128,000. Real rates change, so check current census data.

Sampling studies part of a population. Simple random sampling gives every unit an equal chance; systematic sampling takes every kth unit; stratified sampling draws within groups; cluster sampling takes whole groups.

Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, always between 0 and 1. If 12 of 40 households have piped water, the probability of picking one at random is 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3.

keyPoints: Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle value; mode = most frequent value.
Standard deviation = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n) for a whole population.
Crude birth rate = births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000.
Index number = current value ÷ base value × 100.
Compound projection: P = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ.
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, between 0 and 1.

en.title: Maps, Cartography and GIS Basics
en.short: Map scale, projections, coordinates, thematic maps, GIS layers, GPS and remote sensing.

sections.heading: Scale and maps
sections.text:
A map is a simplified drawing of part of the Earth; cartography is the art and science of making maps. Map scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance. A representative fraction of 1:50,000 means one map unit represents 50,000 ground units. A scale bar stays correct when a map is resized.

Example: 4 cm on a 1:50,000 map is 4 × 50,000 = 200,000 cm = 2 km. Area scales by the square, so 1 cm² is 0.25 km². Large-scale maps show small areas in detail; small-scale maps show large areas with less detail.

sections.heading: Projections and coordinates
sections.text:
The Earth is curved; maps are flat. A map projection is a set of rules for turning positions on the Earth into positions on a flat map. Every projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction. A conformal projection preserves local angles and shapes; an equal-area projection preserves area; a compromise projection balances distortions.

Latitude and longitude are angles measured from the Earth’s centre. Projected coordinates are eastings and northings in metres. A projected coordinate reference system (CRS) combines a datum, which fixes the Earth model, with a projection. Mixing CRSs misaligns layers.

sections.heading: Layers and GIS
sections.text:
A GIS (geographic information system) stores spatial data in layers. Each layer holds one feature type: points such as wells, lines such as roads, polygons such as wards, or raster cells. An attribute table records facts about each feature.

Basic operations describe places. Overlay combines layers; buffer draws a zone at a set distance; clip cuts a layer to an area; dissolve merges features with the same value; a spatial query selects by location. A thematic map shows one attribute, such as population density by ward. Choropleth maps shade areas by class; classes change the message.

sections.heading: GPS and images
sections.text:
GPS (Global Positioning System) uses satellites to give position. Accuracy varies with buildings and sky view.

Remote sensing images come from satellites or drones; pixel size, revisit time and spectral bands set what they can show.

keyPoints: Map scale = map distance ÷ ground distance; 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 0.5 km on the ground.
Ground distance = map distance × scale denominator; area scales by the square of the linear scale.
Every map projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction; choose one that preserves the property you need.
A projected coordinate reference system combines a datum and a projection; mixing CRSs misaligns layers.
GIS stores spatial data as layers with attribute tables; basic operations include overlay, buffer, clip, dissolve and spatial query.
GPS gives position from satellites; remote sensing images differ in pixel size, revisit time and spectral bands.

en.title: Urban Economics for Planners
en.short: Location choices, bid rent, agglomeration, housing and transport markets, and market failure.

sections.heading: Location and bid rent
sections.text:
Urban economics studies how firms and households choose locations and how those choices shape land use and prices. Firms trade transport costs against land rent; households trade commuting and space against amenities. Bid rent is the maximum rent a user can pay at a place while keeping normal profit or utility. Bid-rent curves usually fall with distance from the centre because travel costs rise.

Land goes to the highest bidder. Example: a shop bids 100,000 − 15,000d naira per month, where d is km from the centre; housing bids 40,000 − 5,000d. They are equal when 100,000 − 15,000d = 40,000 − 5,000d, so 60,000 = 10,000d and d = 6 km. At 6 km both bid 10,000 naira. Inside 6 km the shop wins; outside, housing wins.

sections.heading: Agglomeration
sections.text: Agglomeration economies are savings from firms and people locating close together. They come from sharing suppliers and infrastructure, pooling labour, and knowledge spillovers. They help explain large cities and clusters. Crowding, congestion and high rents are diseconomies that limit city size. Planners support clusters with transport, serviced land and utilities, while managing the downsides.

sections.heading: Housing and transport
sections.text: Housing markets match demand and supply of dwellings. Demand depends on income, household size, prices and access; supply responds slowly because building takes time and land is fixed in the short run. Transport markets connect homes to jobs. Road space is often unpriced, so each driver ignores the delay imposed on others. This negative externality is a cost borne by third parties. Congestion charging or bus priority can reduce it.

sections.heading: Market failure and policy
sections.text: Market failure occurs when prices do not reflect costs and benefits. Externalities and public goods are examples. A public good is non-rival, so one person’s use does not reduce another’s, and non-excludable, so people cannot be kept out. Street lighting is an example. Planning uses economics to set land-use rules, protect open space, coordinate infrastructure and compare project benefits with costs. Values matter, so economics informs choices rather than deciding them.

keyPoints: Bid rent is the maximum rent a user can pay at a location while covering costs or reaching a target utility.
Land tends to go to the highest bidder, so bid-rent curves help explain land-use patterns.
Agglomeration economies arise from sharing, labour pooling and knowledge spillovers; congestion and high rents are diseconomies.
Housing supply is slow to adjust in the short run, and unpriced road space creates congestion externalities.
Market failure includes externalities, public goods, monopoly and poor information; public goods are non-rival and non-excludable.
In a simple two-use model, set bids equal: 100,000 − 15,000d = 40,000 − 5,000d gives d = 6 km.

en.title: Urban Sociology and Community Studies
en.short: How city social structure, inequality, migration, family, informality and exclusion shape planning.

sections.heading: Social structure and inequality
sections.text: Social structure is the pattern of institutions, roles and relationships that organises city life: households, markets, schools, religious bodies and government. Inequality is the uneven access to income, housing, land, services and power. It appears in rent burdens, insecure tenure, long journeys to work and unequal school quality. Planners measure it with household surveys and service maps, but numbers must be read with local history.

sections.heading: Migration and family life
sections.text: Migration is movement between places, whether rural to urban, city to city or across borders. Push factors include low rural incomes and conflict; pull factors include jobs and services. Migrants may send remittances home and may live in crowded rental housing. Family life changes as extended kin networks adapt to city distances. Community can mean a place, a shared identity or an interest group, so planners should ask which community they mean.

sections.heading: Informality and exclusion
sections.text: Informality describes work, housing and services operating outside formal regulation. It is not simply illegality: a trader may be licensed but a settlement may lack approved layouts. Informal settlements often have insecure tenure and poor drainage. Gender is the socially constructed roles and expectations placed on women and men. It shapes mobility, safety, land access and voice in meetings. Social exclusion is being shut out of services, decisions or social life, and it can combine with poverty, disability or migration status.

sections.heading: Studying communities
sections.text: Community studies use household surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation, transect walks, participatory mapping and secondary data. Good practice uses local languages, consent, safe storage of data and feedback to residents. Case: in a fictional Nigerian neighbourhood, a drainage upgrade would displace market traders. A survey and focus groups show that women tenants would lose both stall and home. Planners reroute the drain and arrange temporary stalls. This is an illustrative case, not a real project.

keyPoints: Social structure is the pattern of institutions, roles and relationships; inequality is uneven access to income, housing, services and power.
Migration can bring remittances and labour but also crowded housing and insecure tenure.
Community can be a place, a shared identity or an interest group, so define it before planning.
Informality is a continuum, not simply illegality, and often involves insecure tenure and poor services.
Gender and social exclusion shape mobility, safety, land access and voice.
Understand communities through mixed, ethical methods: surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation and participatory mapping.

en.title: Environmental Systems and Sustainable Development
en.short: Ecology, hydrology, climate and soil in cities, carrying capacity, pollution, climate risk and sustainable planning.

sections.heading: Ecology and soil
sections.text: Ecology is the study of how living things relate to each other and to their environment. In an urban region, ecosystems include parks, wetlands, rivers, farmland and built land. They provide ecosystem services: clean air, shade, drainage, food and habitat. Soil is a mixture of minerals, organic matter, water and air. It supports plants, stores water and carbon, and filters pollutants. Covering soil with impermeable surfaces such as concrete and asphalt, called sealing, reduces infiltration (water soaking into the ground) and increases surface runoff.

sections.heading: Water and climate
sections.text: Hydrology is the study of the movement and storage of water: rainfall, infiltration, runoff, groundwater and evaporation. Urban growth creates impervious surfaces such as roofs and roads. More water runs off quickly, less soaks into the ground, and floods and pollution become more likely. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a place. The urban heat island effect makes cities warmer than the countryside because concrete and asphalt store heat and vegetation is scarce. Climate risk is the chance of harm from hazards such as floods, heat and drought. Planners assess exposure (what is in the hazard’s path), vulnerability (how badly it could be harmed) and adaptive capacity (how well it can cope).

sections.heading: Carrying capacity and pollution
sections.text: Carrying capacity is the maximum population or activity an area can support without degrading its environmental systems. It depends on water, land, waste absorption, energy, imports, technology and lifestyles, so it is not a single fixed number. Pollution is the release of harmful substances or energy into air, water or soil; noise and solid waste are also pollution. Example: a made-up town has a reliable water supply of 6,000 m³ per day (6,000,000 litres) and uses 150 litres per person per day. Its water-based capacity is 6,000,000 ÷ 150 = 40,000 people. Other limits may be lower.

sections.heading: Sustainable development
sections.text: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations, following the Brundtland report of 1987. In planning it means integrating environmental protection, economic activity and social equity. Practical aims include compact mixed-use settlements, protected wetlands and farmland, green infrastructure (parks, trees and wetlands that manage water and heat), public transport, waste reduction and climate adaptation. Environmental standards differ by country, so check current national laws and agencies.

keyPoints: Ecology studies relationships between living things and their environment; urban ecosystems provide ecosystem services such as drainage and shade.
Covering soil with impermeable surfaces (sealing) reduces infiltration and increases runoff, raising flood risk.
Climate risk depends on exposure, vulnerability and adaptive capacity, not only on the hazard.
Carrying capacity is the maximum population or activity an area can support without degrading its systems.
Water-based carrying capacity = daily supply ÷ daily use per person, in the same units; for 6,000 m³ per day and 150 litres per person per day it is 40,000 people.
Sustainable development integrates environmental, economic and social goals and requires checking current national standards.

en.title: Site Planning, Graphics and Site Analysis
en.short: Reading plans and sections, surveying a site, analysing slope, drainage, access and orientation, and presenting a layout.

sections.heading: Plans and sections
sections.text: A plan is a view from above, drawn to scale. A section is a vertical cut through the site or building. An elevation shows an outside face. Plans locate things in two dimensions; sections show heights and levels. Always read the scale, the north arrow and the title block. A scale of 1:200 means one unit on paper represents 200 units on the ground. Draw walls, paths and boundaries with line weights that show what is cut and what is beyond.

sections.heading: Survey and slope
sections.text: A site survey records boundaries, levels, trees, services and neighbouring buildings. Contours join points of equal height. Water flows downhill at right angles to contours. Slope is vertical rise divided by horizontal run. Example: a plot in Ibadan falls 1.5 m over 20 m. Slope = 1.5 ÷ 20 = 0.075, or 7.5%, or 1 in 13.3. Steep sites need terracing and careful drainage. Check the local survey and planning rules; they differ by country.

sections.heading: Site analysis
sections.text: Site analysis turns survey data into opportunities and constraints. Access: where can vehicles and pedestrians enter safely? Orientation: sun and prevailing wind affect comfort. In hot climates, a long east-west axis reduces east and west wall heating; in cooler climates, south-facing windows in the northern hemisphere collect winter sun. Drainage: keep buildings out of low spots and direct water to approved drains. Constraints include setbacks, easements, flood risk, noise, soil and protected trees. Design codes and professional registration differ by country, so check the current local authority and professional body.

sections.heading: Presentation
sections.text: A site layout should be clear to a reader who was not on the site. Include a title block, north arrow, scale bar, legend and dimensions. Use consistent scales and hatching. Show existing and proposed work differently. A short written note explains the analysis and the design decisions. Keep drawings tidy and check that every symbol is explained.

keyPoints: A plan is a view from above; a section is a vertical cut; both must state their scale.
Slope = vertical rise ÷ horizontal run, shown as a ratio, percentage or angle.
Water flows downhill at right angles to contours, so drainage follows the fall of the land.
Site analysis weighs access, orientation, drainage and constraints before layout.
Orientation advice depends on climate and hemisphere, not on one universal rule.
Design codes, survey standards and professional registration differ by country; check the current local source.

en.title: Urban Form and Land Use Patterns
en.short: Streets, blocks, plots and public space; density, sprawl and land-use patterns; tools for mapping city growth.

sections.heading: Elements of form
sections.text: Urban form is the physical arrangement of a city: its streets, blocks, plots, buildings and public spaces. A street network is the pattern of roads and paths. A block is land enclosed by streets. A plot is an individual parcel with boundaries and a use. Public space includes streets, squares, parks and open land that people can reach. Figure-ground maps show buildings as solid and open space as empty, making the pattern easy to compare.

sections.heading: Density and sprawl
sections.text:
Density is an amount per unit area, such as dwellings per hectare (ha). Gross density counts all land in the area. Net density counts only the land used for the stated purpose, often excluding major roads and open space. Floor area ratio (FAR) is total floor area ÷ plot area. Sprawl is low-density outward growth, often with separated land uses and heavy car dependence.

Example: a site 400 m × 500 m = 200,000 m² = 20 ha holds 300 homes. Gross density = 300 ÷ 20 = 15 homes/ha. If 4 ha is roads and open space, net area = 16 ha, so net density = 300 ÷ 16 = 18.75 homes/ha.

sections.heading: Land-use patterns
sections.text: Land-use patterns describe where activities are placed: residential, commercial, industrial, institutional, open space and mixed use. A monocentric city has a strong centre; a polycentric city has several centres. Corridor growth follows transport routes. Mixed use puts compatible activities close together. Zoning rules differ by country and city, so check the local plan.

sections.heading: Mapping and comparing
sections.text: Planners use land-use maps, figure-ground maps, street-network maps and density maps. A transect is a cross-section from centre to edge showing changes in form and density. Aerial photographs and satellite images from different dates show growth. To compare cities fairly, use the same land-use classes, scale and date, and record the source.

keyPoints: Urban form is the physical pattern of streets, blocks, plots, buildings and public space.
Density = amount ÷ area; gross density counts all land, net density counts only the relevant land.
Floor area ratio = total floor area ÷ plot area.
Sprawl is low-density outward growth, often with separated uses and car dependence.
Land-use maps, figure-ground maps and density maps help compare city growth.
Use the same classes, scale and date when comparing maps.

en.title: Planning Theory and the Public Interest
en.short: Planning theories, public interest debates and the planner’s role in decisions.

sections.heading: Rational and incremental
sections.text: The rational-comprehensive model asks planners to define goals, list all options, predict consequences and choose the best. Herbert Simon argued that real planners face bounded rationality: limited time, information and attention. Charles Lindblom’s incrementalism says decisions usually adjust existing policies by small steps, because agreement is easier and mistakes are reversible. It is criticised for protecting existing power. The rational model is a useful ideal, not a description of practice.

sections.heading: Advocacy and communication
sections.text: Advocacy planning, associated with Paul Davidoff, says planners should speak for groups left out of decisions, not claim neutrality. Communicative planning, linked to Patsy Healey and John Forester, sees planning as dialogue. It seeks shared understanding through open argument, but critics note that unequal power can distort talk. Power can set the agenda before talk begins.

sections.heading: Justice and public interest
sections.text: Justice-oriented theory asks whether a plan reduces unfairness. Susan Fainstein’s just city judges plans by equity, democracy and diversity. There is no single public interest. Public interest is a claim about what serves the community, and groups define it differently. It is contested: a road may serve commuters and harm traders. Planners may act as technicians, advocates, mediators or political advisers. Professional registration differs by country, for example TOPREC registers town planners in Nigeria, so check local rules.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider a made-up Nigerian town. The council proposes a new market. Planner Aisha prepares a rational report. Trader Musa fears losing his stall. An incremental plan might test a temporary site first. Advocacy would have a planner speak for Musa’s group and help it present evidence. Communicative planning would hold a public meeting with equal speaking time. A justice check asks who gains and who bears the cost. The planner’s role changes with each approach.

keyPoints: The rational-comprehensive model is an ideal; bounded rationality and incrementalism describe real practice.
Incrementalism adjusts existing policy in small steps and can protect existing power.
Advocacy planning asks planners to speak for excluded groups rather than claim neutrality.
Communicative planning treats planning as dialogue, but unequal power can distort it.
Justice-oriented theory judges plans by equity, democracy and diversity, as in Fainstein’s just city.
There is no single public interest; planners may act as technicians, advocates, mediators or advisers, and local professional rules differ by country.

en.title: Land Use Planning and Zoning
en.short: Surveys, forecasts, land allocation, zoning, density, mixed use and enforcement.

sections.heading: Surveys and forecasts
sections.text: A land-use survey records what exists: parcels, uses, floorspace, vacancies, infrastructure and constraints. It feeds a forecast of future needs for housing, employment, transport and open space. Common methods are trend extrapolation, the cohort-component method (projecting population by age and sex), and household or employment projections. Forecasts are uncertain, so planners test high and low scenarios and update them. In Nigeria, state planning authorities and local governments collect such data, but practice varies.

sections.heading: Allocation methods
sections.text: Land allocation decides which activities go where. Suitability analysis maps opportunities and constraints, such as slope, flood risk, access and services, then scores sites. Multi-criteria evaluation weights those factors. Allocation must consider capacity, demand and equity. A worked example: a 2 ha site is planned for 80 dwellings with 4 people per household. Gross density, counting all site land, is 80 ÷ 2 = 40 dwellings per hectare. Population density is (80 × 4) ÷ 2 = 160 persons per hectare.

sections.heading: Zoning and subdivision
sections.text: Zoning divides land into zones and sets permitted uses and development standards. Euclidean zoning, common in the United States, separates residential, commercial and industrial uses. England uses use classes that group similar uses and allow some changes without a new permission; the details change, so check current rules. Subdivision control governs dividing land into plots: access, plot size, services and layout. It is separate from zoning but works with it.

sections.heading: Density and enforcement
sections.text: Density controls how much development is allowed on land. It can be expressed as dwellings per hectare, plot ratio (floor area ÷ site area) or coverage (built footprint ÷ site area). Mixed use combines compatible uses to shorten trips and support local services. Development control checks applications against the plan and zoning; enforcement acts on unauthorised work. Tools include stop notices, fines and demolition orders, but powers differ by country. In Nigeria, planning permission is required from the relevant state or local planning authority, and enforcement can be weak where capacity and political pressure are problems.

keyPoints: A land-use survey records existing uses and constraints; forecasts estimate future housing, employment and transport needs.
Suitability analysis and multi-criteria evaluation help allocate land, but capacity, demand and equity also matter.
Gross density = dwellings ÷ site area; population density = residents ÷ site area; plot ratio = floor area ÷ site area.
Zoning sets permitted uses and standards, while subdivision control governs how land is divided into plots.
Mixed use can shorten trips and support services, but compatible uses and servicing must be checked.
Development control and enforcement need clear plans, capacity and consistent action; rules differ by country.

en.title: Urban Design and Placemaking
en.short: Streets, public spaces, legibility, safety, accessibility and design guidelines.

sections.heading: Streets and public realm
sections.text: Urban design shapes the public realm: the streets, squares, parks and open spaces that people share. A street is not only a pipe for traffic. It is a social and economic space, so design should balance movement with sitting, trading, shade and access to buildings. Mixed-use areas put homes, shops, offices and services close together. This supports walking and local trade, but planners must manage noise, waste and delivery conflicts. Active frontages, meaning doors and windows facing the street, make walking more interesting and safer. Placemaking is the process of working with users to improve a place, not just designing it for them.

sections.heading: Legibility, safety and scale
sections.text: Legibility is how easily people understand and navigate a place. Kevin Lynch described five elements: paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. Clear routes, visible landmarks and well-defined edges help residents and visitors find their way. Safety depends on natural surveillance: people can see and be seen in streets and open spaces. Jane Jacobs argued that busy, mixed streets with eyes on the street support safety. Accessibility means removing physical, sensory and economic barriers so that children, older people and people with disabilities can use a place. Human scale means details and speeds suit people on foot, not only cars.

sections.heading: Guidelines and planning goals
sections.text: Design guidelines translate planning aims into practical rules for building lines, street widths, heights, setbacks, frontages and public space. They may appear in masterplans, street design manuals or form-based codes, which regulate the shape of places rather than only land use. Standards differ by country, so check the current local code and professional registration rules. A made-up case: in a Nigerian town, Amina Street has a market, a school and homes. Widening one footpath, adding shade, a crossing and a small square with a landmark would improve safety, access and trade without removing the street’s mixed use. Urban design supports planning goals such as compactness, public health, local economy and climate resilience.

keyPoints: Urban design shapes the public realm, including streets, squares, parks and open spaces.
Mixed use brings activities together and supports walking, but needs conflict management.
Legibility, after Kevin Lynch, uses paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks.
Natural surveillance and active frontages help streets feel safer.
Accessibility and human scale make places usable for all ages and abilities.
Design guidelines turn planning goals into local rules, and codes differ by country.

en.title: Housing Policy and Affordability
en.short: Housing markets, tenure, affordability measures, social and rental housing, informal settlements and upgrading.

sections.heading: Housing markets and tenure
sections.text:
A housing market matches demand for dwellings with supply of land, finance and construction. Prices and rents rise when demand outruns supply, especially where land or planning permission is scarce.

Tenure is the legal right by which a household occupies a home. Common forms include owner-occupation, private rental, social rental, customary tenure and informal occupation.

Tenure shapes security, maintenance and access to credit, so policy must consider it, not only prices.

sections.heading: Measuring affordability
sections.text:
Affordability compares housing cost with household income. Two simple measures are the rent-to-income ratio and the house-price-to-income ratio. A third is residual income: income left after housing for food, transport and other needs. Definitions and thresholds differ by country and agency, so state the measure and source.

Example: a household earns 120,000 per month and pays rent of 36,000. Rent-to-income = 36,000 ÷ 120,000 = 0.30, or 30%. Residual income = 120,000 − 36,000 = 84,000 per month. If the home costs 4,800,000 and annual income is 1,440,000, price-to-income = 4,800,000 ÷ 1,440,000 = 3.33. The common 30% benchmark is not universal.

sections.heading: Social and rental housing
sections.text:
Social housing is subsidised housing provided or enabled by government for households that cannot afford market rents. Rental housing includes private and social tenancies. Demand-side tools such as housing allowances help tenants pay rent. Supply-side tools include public building, land subsidies and incentives for private rental.

Rent control can protect sitting tenants, but economists warn it may reduce new rental supply and maintenance; effects depend on design and enforcement. Allocation rules and tenancy laws are country-specific.

sections.heading: Informal settlements and tools
sections.text:
Slums and informal settlements are areas where residents lack secure tenure, safe water, sanitation or compliance with building rules. In-situ upgrading improves services, roads, drainage and tenure without mass relocation. Sites-and-services schemes provide serviced plots, and households build gradually.

Policy tools include land release, infrastructure, subsidies, titling and building codes. Legal powers to regularise tenure, control rents, evict or acquire land differ by country. Name the jurisdiction and check current law.

keyPoints: Tenure is the legal right to occupy a home; owner-occupation, rental, customary and informal tenure carry different security and credit access.
Rent-to-income = rent ÷ household income; price-to-income = house price ÷ annual household income.
Residual income = household income − housing cost; it shows what is left for other needs.
Affordability thresholds differ by country and agency, so state the measure and source.
Social housing and housing allowances are policy tools; rent control can protect tenants but may reduce rental supply and maintenance.
Slum upgrading and sites-and-services improve services and tenure; legal powers over rents, eviction, titling and land acquisition are country-specific.

en.title: Transport Planning and Mobility
en.short: Travel demand, trip distribution, public transport, walking, cycling, road hierarchy, parking, land use and appraisal.

sections.heading: Travel demand
sections.text: Travel demand is the number and pattern of trips people and goods make. It is derived: people travel to reach work, school, shops or services. A trip is one one-way movement from origin to destination. Trip generation estimates trips from a development, often as trips per dwelling or employee per day. Use local surveyed rates. Example: 400 dwellings at an assumed 2.5 trips per dwelling per day give 400 × 2.5 = 1,000 trips per day. If 10% occur in the peak hour, that is 100 peak-hour trips.

sections.heading: Distribution and modes
sections.text: Trip distribution decides where trips go. Gravity models assume flows between zones rise with trip ends and fall with travel time or cost. Public transport needs frequency, capacity, reliability and fare integration. Walking and cycling need safe footways, crossings, cycle lanes and connected streets. Road hierarchy separates movement from access: arterial roads carry through traffic, collector roads link neighbourhoods, local streets give property access. Design speeds and widths differ by country and code.

sections.heading: Parking and land use
sections.text: Parking policy manages demand. Cheap abundant parking encourages car use; scarce parking can harm business. Tools include supply limits, pricing, shared parking and park-and-ride. Land-use transport integration places dense, mixed-use development near public transport and makes walking and cycling convenient. Transit-oriented development clusters housing, jobs and shops around stations. Parking and road standards are country-specific; check the local code.

sections.heading: Appraisal
sections.text: Appraisal compares options before money is committed. Cost-benefit analysis values benefits and costs in money and discounts future flows: NPV = Σ (B − C) ÷ (1 + r)^t. Multi-criteria analysis adds impacts hard to price, such as heritage, access and environment. Example: a bus priority scheme costs $2,000,000 and saves 200,000 travel hours a year. At an assumed $2 per hour, annual benefit is $400,000. Over 10 years undiscounted that is $4,000,000; discounted at 10%, present value is about $2,457,000, so the benefit-cost ratio is about 1.23. Use official appraisal guidance for the country.

keyPoints: Travel demand is derived from activities, so land-use decisions shape trip numbers and patterns.
Trip generation: daily trips = units × trip rate; use local surveyed rates.
Trip distribution matches origins and destinations, often with gravity models that fall with travel time or cost.
Road hierarchy separates through movement from access, and design standards differ by country.
Parking and land-use integration can reduce car dependence by placing dense mixed uses near public transport and safe walking and cycling routes.
Appraisal: NPV = Σ (B − C) ÷ (1 + r)^t; cost-benefit analysis uses money values, while multi-criteria analysis covers hard-to-price impacts.

en.title: Infrastructure and Utilities Planning
en.short: Water, sanitation, drainage, waste, energy and telecoms: standards, demand, phasing and land-use coordination.

sections.heading: Service standards
sections.text: Infrastructure means networks and facilities that serve land: water supply, sanitation, drainage, solid waste, energy and telecommunications. A service standard states the level of service a system should provide, such as water quality, pressure, reliability or collection frequency. Standards differ by country. In Nigeria, the Nigerian Standard for Drinking Water Quality (NSDWQ) is issued by the Standards Organisation of Nigeria; World Health Organization guidelines are international advice, not local law. Check the national standard.

sections.heading: Demand estimation
sections.text:
Demand estimation converts population and land use into quantities. For water, demand = population × per capita demand, plus allowances for institutions, industry and losses. Per capita figures vary by country, climate and income, so use a current local planning figure.

Example: a new district of 20,000 people is planned at 120 litres per person per day. Base demand = 20,000 × 120 = 2,400,000 litres per day. Add 20% for institutions and losses: 2,400,000 × 1.20 = 2,880,000 litres per day. Divide by 86,400 seconds per day: 2,880,000 ÷ 86,400 = 33.3 litres per second.

sections.heading: Networks and phasing
sections.text:
Sanitation, drainage, solid waste, energy and telecommunications each need space. Sanitation may mean sewers, septic tanks or on-site systems; drainage needs channels and flood paths; solid waste needs collection routes, transfer stations and disposal sites; energy needs substations and corridors; telecommunications need masts, ducts and fibre routes. Planners reserve land and rights of way (legal access rights), and protect easements (legal rights to run pipes or cables across land) and buffer zones. Coordination with land use means matching capacity to zoning density and keeping noisy or odorous facilities away from homes.

Phasing means building in stages as demand grows, so capital is not idle. Install trunk mains and drainage before or with roads, then extend services as plots are occupied. Water, sewer, power and fibre should share a corridor, or a common trench where standards allow, which avoids repeated excavation. The planning authority, utility agencies and developers agree a servicing plan before land is released for building.

keyPoints: Infrastructure planning covers water, sanitation, drainage, solid waste, energy and telecommunications.
Service standards set levels such as quality, pressure and reliability, and they vary by country; check the current national standard.
Water demand = population × per capita demand plus allowances for institutions, industry and losses.
In the worked example, 20,000 people at 120 litres per person per day plus 20% gives 2,880,000 litres per day, or 33.3 litres per second.
Reserve land, rights of way and buffer zones, and match utility capacity to land-use density.
Phase infrastructure with development and coordinate utility corridors to avoid repeated excavation.

en.title: Regional Planning and Development
en.short: Regional disparities, growth poles, rural-urban linkages, regional analysis and balanced cross-border planning.
keywords: Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning

sections.heading: Regional disparities
sections.text: Regional disparities are differences between areas in income, jobs, services and living conditions. They arise from resource endowment, history, agglomeration and policy. Agglomeration means firms and people clustering because proximity lowers costs, which can pull activity into large cities. Regional planning studies these gaps and asks whether public investment should be concentrated or spread. Balanced development does not mean identical regions; it means reducing severe gaps in access to work and basic services.

sections.heading: Growth poles and linkages
sections.text: A growth pole is a centre or key industry chosen for investment in the hope that benefits spread to its region. The idea comes from François Perroux. Benefits may spread through jobs, purchases and migration, but backwash effects can drain skilled people and capital from smaller places, as Gunnar Myrdal warned. Rural-urban linkages are the flows between countryside and towns: food, labour, remittances, services and information. Market towns often link farmers to larger markets.

sections.heading: Regional analysis and plans
sections.text: Regional analysis compares areas using indicators such as population, employment and service access. A location quotient (LQ) measures concentration. LQ = (regional share of a sector) ÷ (national share of that sector). Example: a region has 60,000 manufacturing jobs out of 500,000 total, so 12%. The nation has 2,000,000 out of 20,000,000, so 10%. LQ = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2, showing above-average concentration. A regional plan then sets spatial strategy, investment priorities and coordination between sectors.

sections.heading: Balanced and cross-border planning
sections.text: Balanced development uses transfers, infrastructure and growth-centre investment to widen opportunity. In Nigeria, the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning (formerly the National Planning Commission) coordinates national planning, state ministries responsible for physical planning prepare state spatial plans, and local government councils handle local matters. In South Africa, municipalities prepare Integrated Development Plans, their main plans for local development. Cross-border planning is needed for shared rivers, transport corridors and migration; ECOWAS and the Lake Chad Basin Commission are examples of bodies that coordinate such work. Check current national rules, because institutions and plan requirements change.

keyPoints: Regional disparities are differences in income, jobs and services between areas, shaped by endowment, history, agglomeration and policy.
Growth pole theory expects investment in a centre or key industry to spread benefits, but backwash effects can concentrate them.
Rural-urban linkages include flows of food, labour, money, services and information between countryside and towns.
Location quotient = regional sector share ÷ national sector share; LQ above 1 shows concentration.
Balanced development aims to reduce severe gaps, not to make all regions identical.
Cross-border planning needs shared institutions; examples include ECOWAS and the Lake Chad Basin Commission.

en.title: Environmental Planning and Impact Assessment
en.short: EIA process, screening, scoping, baselines, mitigation, monitoring, climate resilience and environmental justice.

sections.heading: EIA and SEA
sections.text: Environmental impact assessment (EIA) predicts the environmental effects of a project before approval. Strategic environmental assessment (SEA) applies similar thinking to plans, programmes and policies. Laws differ: Nigeria’s Environmental Impact Assessment Act 1992; South Africa’s National Environmental Management Act 1998 with EIA regulations; Kenya’s Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act 1999; Ghana’s Environmental Assessment Regulations 1999 (LI 1652); the EU EIA Directive 2011/92/EU; and the US National Environmental Policy Act 1969. Check current amendments and local thresholds.

sections.heading: Screening to monitoring
sections.text: Screening decides whether an EIA is needed, using thresholds, sensitive locations or case-by-case review. Scoping sets the terms of reference and the key issues. Baseline studies record existing air, water, soil, ecology and people. Impact prediction compares the with-project and without-project conditions. Mitigation follows a hierarchy: avoid, minimise, restore, offset. An environmental management plan (EMP) assigns actions, costs and responsibilities. Monitoring checks actual effects and compliance; review and public participation run throughout.

sections.heading: Climate and justice
sections.text: Plan-making should assess climate hazards and vulnerability, not only project emissions. Climate resilience means preparing for floods, heat, drought and sea-level rise. Green infrastructure uses nature-based systems such as urban trees, parks, permeable paving and sustainable drainage (SUDS) to manage water and heat. Environmental justice asks whether poor or minority communities carry more pollution and less access to green space, and whether they are heard.

sections.heading: Small case
sections.text: A made-up estate near a wetland in Lagos: screening may require EIA because of wetland and flood risk; scoping focuses on drainage and livelihoods; baseline surveys water and ecology; mitigation avoids building on the floodplain, keeps buffers and uses SUDS; monitoring tracks water quality. Planners should check Nigeria’s current EIA Act and agency practice.

keyPoints: EIA predicts a project’s environmental effects before approval, while SEA applies to plans and programmes.
Screening decides whether EIA is needed; scoping sets the issues and terms of reference.
Baseline studies describe existing conditions; mitigation follows avoid, minimise, restore, offset; monitoring checks actual effects.
EIA laws and thresholds differ by country, so name the law and check current rules.
Climate resilience and green infrastructure reduce hazard exposure and can bring co-benefits.
Environmental justice checks fair distribution of environmental burdens and benefits and inclusive participation.

en.title: Planning Law and Development Control
en.short: Legal basis, development plans, permission, subdivision, building control, enforcement and appeals.

sections.heading: Legal basis and plans
sections.text: Planning law is the statutes, regulations and court decisions that control land use. It authorises public bodies to prepare development plans and decide applications. A development plan is a statutory document of land-use policies and proposals, such as a local plan in England or a master plan in Nigeria. It guides, but does not always bind, decisions. In federal countries, powers may be split: Nigeria’s Urban and Regional Planning Act 1992 gives a national framework, while states and local governments make plans and grant approvals. England’s main Act is the Town and Country Planning Act 1990.

sections.heading: Permission and subdivision
sections.text: Planning permission is formal approval to carry out development, usually building, engineering, mining or a material change of use. The local planning authority may grant, refuse or attach conditions. Subdivision control is separate: it approves dividing land into plots and checks access, services and layout. Building control is also separate: it checks structural safety, fire, drainage and sanitation under a building code.

sections.heading: Enforcement and appeals
sections.text: Development control is the day-to-day work of checking applications and enforcing rules. If development starts without permission or a condition is broken, the authority may serve an enforcement notice requiring the breach to be remedied, for example by stopping the use or removing buildings. Appeals usually go to a tribunal, inspector or court. In England, the Planning Inspectorate decides appeals. In Nigeria, appeal bodies and time limits vary by state. A made-up case: Ada in Enugu converts a house to a shop without permission. The authority serves an enforcement notice; she may appeal under state law.

sections.heading: Country differences
sections.text: Systems differ in who decides. In England, local planning authorities decide most applications, and the Secretary of State can call in major cases. In Nigeria, state planning authorities and local governments share roles. Some countries use zoning ordinances; others use discretionary permission. Always check the current national and state law, because names, forms and time limits change.

keyPoints: Planning law is made up of statutes, regulations and court decisions that authorise plans and control development.
A development plan guides decisions but does not always bind the decision-maker.
Planning permission, subdivision approval and building control are separate approvals.
An enforcement notice requires a breach to be remedied, for example by stopping the use or removing buildings.
Appeals go to a tribunal, inspector or court, and the body and time limits differ by country.
Always check the current national and state law; do not rely on another country’s rules.

en.title: Urban Land Administration and Property
en.short: Cadastre, land registration, tenure types, land markets, compulsory acquisition, compensation and property tax.

sections.heading: Cadastre and registration
sections.text: A cadastre is a parcel by parcel record of land: boundaries, area, holder and use, usually on maps. Land registration is the legal record of rights in land. In deed registration the state keeps copies of documents but does not guarantee the title. In title registration, such as the Torrens system that began in South Australia in the nineteenth century, the register itself is evidence of title. A strong system links the map to the register.

sections.heading: Tenure types
sections.text:
Tenure is the set of rules by which people hold and use land. Freehold is ownership without a time limit. Leasehold is held for a fixed term, often from the state. Under customary tenure, rights come from a community and are held by families, clans or stools, usually through oral tradition rather than a written register.

National law decides the details. Nigeria’s Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state governor, who grants statutory rights of occupancy for urban land; local governments grant customary rights of occupancy for non-urban land. Ghana’s 1992 Constitution recognises customary ownership, including stool lands. Kenya’s 2010 Constitution classes land as public, private and community.

sections.heading: Markets and acquisition
sections.text:
Land markets transfer rights by sale, lease or inheritance. Secure title can raise land’s value as loan collateral, though studies of titling programmes report mixed results. Compulsory acquisition (eminent domain) lets the state take land for public purposes, under a set procedure and with compensation. In Nigeria, compensation under the Land Use Act is for unexhausted improvements, not the land itself.

Example: a building with replacement cost ₦48,000,000 and 20% depreciation is compensated at 48,000,000 × 0.80 = ₦38,400,000.

sections.heading: Property taxation
sections.text: Property tax is an annual charge on land and buildings, based on rateable value (capital or rental) or on floor area. In Nigeria, local government councils commonly levy tenement or property rates; the base and rate are set locally, so check the current law. Taxes on transfers, such as stamp duty, are separate. Valuation rolls must be updated, and weak enforcement is the usual problem.

keyPoints: A cadastre records parcels; land registration records legal rights.
Title registration makes the register itself evidence of title; deed registration does not.
Tenure types include freehold, leasehold and customary tenure, and national law governs them.
Compulsory acquisition requires a lawful procedure and compensation for losses defined by law.
In Nigeria, compensation under the Land Use Act covers improvements, not the land itself.
Property tax is usually a percentage of rateable value; rates and bases differ by country and locality.

en.title: Community Participation and Social Inclusion
en.short: Stakeholder analysis, participatory methods, inclusion and power in community planning.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and power
sections.text:
Stakeholder analysis identifies people and groups affected by a plan. A power-interest grid plots each group by its power and its interest. High-power, high-interest groups need close engagement; low-power, high-interest groups need support to be heard.

Power is the ability to influence decisions, not only money. Representation is always a question: a community leader may not speak for women, tenants or informal traders. Elite capture happens when a small group takes the benefits or the voice.

sections.heading: Methods and co-production
sections.text:
Participatory methods include focus group discussions, key informant interviews, transect walks, participatory mapping and community meetings. A transect walk is a guided walk across a site with residents, noting features and problems. Consultation asks for views before a decision.

Co-production goes further: residents and officials share design, delivery and monitoring. A charrette is an intensive design workshop. Methods must fit the purpose, because a large public meeting is poor for shy groups. Feedback matters: tell people what changed and why.

sections.heading: Inclusion and informal areas
sections.text:
Gender and disability inclusion means removing barriers to taking part. Hold meetings at safe times and places, offer childcare, use plain language, and provide ramps, sign language and accessible documents. Disaggregate data by sex, age and disability so needs become visible.

In informal settlements, tenure is often unclear and livelihoods are on the street. Work with existing savings groups, traders associations and tenants, and avoid plans that displace people. Upgrading should be co-produced, not imposed.

sections.heading: Case and conflict
sections.text:
In a made-up neighbourhood in Ibadan, Nigeria, a road upgrade affects traders, a school and a mosque. A stakeholder map shows traders have high interest but low formal power. A transect walk and a women-only focus group reveal that a drainage line would remove stalls.

The plan is changed to keep the stalls and add a school ramp. The council keeps a feedback log. Conflict is normal; transparent rules, independent chairs and mediation help. Participation without power-sharing can become tokenism, where people are invited but cannot change decisions.

keyPoints: Stakeholder analysis maps who is affected, their interests and their power.
Consultation gathers views; co-production shares design, delivery and monitoring with residents.
Inclusion needs accessible meetings, safe timing and data disaggregated by sex, age and disability.
Informal settlements are best upgraded with existing groups and without displacing livelihoods.
Participation can reproduce inequality unless representation, feedback and conflict handling are managed.

en.title: GIS and Spatial Analysis for Planning
en.short: Spatial data quality, suitability and network analysis, remote sensing, map design and ethics.

sections.heading: Data capture and quality
sections.text: Spatial data have a location: points, lines, polygons or pixels. Capture uses field survey and GNSS (global navigation satellite systems such as GPS), digitising, remote sensing, and administrative or crowdsourced records. Quality includes positional and attribute accuracy, completeness, consistency, resolution and currency. Metadata records source, date, projection and processing; topology rules check that polygons close and lines connect. Poor input gives confident but wrong maps.

sections.heading: Suitability and networks
sections.text: Suitability analysis asks where an activity fits. In weighted overlay, each criterion is scored on a common scale, given a weight, and summed. A constraint, such as a flood zone, can mask out land. Example: weights 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2; a site scores 8, 6 and 4 out of 10. Weighted score = 0.5×8 + 0.3×6 + 0.2×4 = 4 + 1.8 + 0.8 = 6.6 out of 10. Network analysis treats roads or pipes as edges and junctions as nodes. It finds shortest paths, service areas and accessibility, meaning how easily people reach jobs, schools or clinics. Impedance is travel cost, such as distance or time.

sections.heading: Remote sensing and maps
sections.text: Remote sensing records reflected or emitted energy without contact. Passive sensors detect reflected sunlight or emitted heat; active sensors such as radar supply their own energy. Images vary in spatial resolution (pixel size), spectral resolution (bands), temporal resolution (revisit time) and radiometric resolution (bit depth). NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red), a greenness index. Map design uses projection, scale, classification, colour, legend, north arrow and source note. Good maps are readable and honest about uncertainty.

sections.heading: Decisions and ethics
sections.text: Spatial decision support combines GIS layers, criteria and scenarios to compare options transparently. It supports judgement; it does not replace it. Ethical use requires consent, privacy, aggregation of small areas to protect individuals, bias checks, licence compliance and respect for community data. Location data can enable surveillance or discrimination, so planners should document assumptions and involve affected people.

keyPoints: Spatial data quality includes positional and attribute accuracy, completeness, consistency, resolution and currency.
Weighted overlay score = Σ(weight × criterion score), with criteria on a common scale.
A constraint masks unsuitable land regardless of its weighted score.
Network analysis uses nodes, edges and impedance to find shortest paths, service areas and accessibility.
NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red).
Ethical spatial data use needs consent, privacy, aggregation, bias checks and licence compliance.

en.title: Project Planning, Appraisal and Implementation
en.short: The project cycle, appraisal, budgets, procurement, scheduling, monitoring and implementation risks.

sections.heading: Cycle and appraisal
sections.text:
A project moves through a cycle: identification, preparation, appraisal, financing, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, then closure. Preparation includes a feasibility study covering technical, financial, economic, environmental, social and institutional issues. Appraisal is an independent review before money is committed.

In cost-benefit analysis, future benefits and costs are discounted to present value. Net present value (NPV) is discounted benefits minus discounted costs. A positive NPV means the project adds value at the chosen discount rate; the rate is a policy choice.

sections.heading: Budget, finance, procurement
sections.text:
A budget sets expected capital and recurrent costs, contingencies and cash flow. Financing may come from government budgets, loans, grants, development banks, public-private partnerships or community contributions. Each source has its own conditions. Loans must be repaid; grants and community contributions are not.

Procurement is buying works, goods and services. Competitive tendering, clear criteria and published awards reduce favouritism. Procurement laws and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, federal procurement is governed by the Public Procurement Act 2007, and COREN registers engineers. Check current national rules.

sections.heading: Scheduling and control
sections.text:
Scheduling turns the work into activities with durations and dependencies. A work breakdown structure divides the project into manageable parts. The critical path method (CPM) finds the longest dependent sequence; delay on the critical path delays completion, while other activities have float. Gantt charts show activities against time.

Monitoring is continuous tracking of inputs, outputs and milestones against plan. Evaluation is a periodic judgement of outcomes and impact, using a baseline and indicators.

sections.heading: Risks and example
sections.text:
Urban and regional projects face land acquisition and compensation disputes, utility relocation, cost overrun, political change, weak capacity, corruption, weather and community opposition. Mitigate with early stakeholder engagement, contingency budgets, phased works, clear contracts and monitoring.

Example: a drainage project costs 10 million now and gives benefits of 6 million a year for two years. At 10%:
NPV = −10 + 6 ÷ 1.1 + 6 ÷ 1.21 = −10 + 5.4545 + 4.9587 = 0.4132 million.
The NPV is positive at that rate. A higher rate could reverse it.

keyPoints: The project cycle runs from identification and preparation through appraisal, financing, implementation and monitoring to evaluation and closure.
Feasibility studies test technical, financial, economic, environmental, social and institutional viability; appraisal reviews them independently.
NPV = Σ (B − C) ÷ (1 + r)^t; a positive NPV means value is added at the chosen discount rate.
Budgets cover capital, recurrent and contingency costs; procurement should use competitive tendering, clear criteria and published awards under country-specific laws.
The critical path is the longest dependent sequence; delay there delays the project, while other activities have float.
Monitoring tracks progress continuously, evaluation judges outcomes against a baseline, and risks such as land disputes and cost overrun need early mitigation.

en.title: Planning Studio: Preparing a Comprehensive Plan
en.short: Team studio from survey and analysis to goals, land-use options, draft plan, implementation and presentation.

sections.heading: Studio sequence
sections.text: A comprehensive plan is a long-range document guiding land use, transport, infrastructure, services and environmental protection for a city or district. In the studio, a team follows a sequence: brief, work plan, survey, analysis, goals, land-use options, draft plan, implementation and presentation. The brief names the client, study area and deliverable. The work plan divides tasks, sets dates and assigns checks. Survey uses primary data, such as site visits and interviews, and secondary data, such as maps and official plans. Record every source so findings can be checked.

sections.heading: Analysis and goals
sections.text: Analysis turns survey data into findings: what is happening, why, and where. The team maps issues and constraints, such as flood-prone land or missing services, and opportunities, such as underused land. Goals are broad statements of what the plan should achieve; objectives are specific and measurable. Goals must come from evidence and the public interest, not team preference. Do not copy goals from another plan without testing them against the local survey.

sections.heading: Options and draft plan
sections.text: Land-use options are alternative spatial arrangements of housing, work, roads, open space and services. The team tests each option against criteria such as access, cost, environmental impact and social inclusion, and records trade-offs. A made-up town Kofar Gari has 100 hectares. Option A gives 60 to housing, 20 to roads, 10 to open space and 10 to services. Option B gives 50, 20, 20 and 10. Both total 100. Option A gives more housing; Option B gives more open space. The chosen option becomes the draft plan: a land-use map, policies and a project schedule. Implementation follows: phasing, budget, responsible agencies and monitoring indicators. A plan without implementation is only a wish list.

sections.heading: Presentation and standards
sections.text: Presentation includes drawings, a report and a public meeting. Explain methods, assumptions and limits, and answer questions. Professional standards differ by country. In Nigeria, the Town Planners Registration Council (TOPREC) regulates town planners; engineers have a separate council (COREN). Check law, codes and registration rules before finalising the plan.

keyPoints: A comprehensive plan is a long-range document guiding land use, transport, infrastructure, services and environmental protection.
The studio sequence is brief, work plan, survey, analysis, goals, land-use options, draft plan, implementation and presentation.
Survey data must be recorded with sources so analysis can be checked.
Goals come from evidence and the public interest; objectives are specific and measurable.
Test land-use options against criteria such as access, cost, environmental impact and social inclusion.
Implementation needs phasing, budget, responsible agencies and monitoring; professional standards and registration differ by country, for example TOPREC in Nigeria.

en.title: Professional Practice, Registration and Ethics
en.short: Registration, planning institutions, public and private practice, ethics, liability and CPD.

sections.heading: Registration and institutions
sections.text:
Professional registration, where it exists, is a legal licence to practise and to use a protected title. It is not the same as membership of a professional institute, though the two often overlap. Requirements differ by country, so check the current regulator.

In Nigeria, the Town Planners Registration Council, TOPREC, is the statutory registration body for town planners. The Nigerian Institute of Town Planners, NITP, is the professional institute. COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria; it is not the planning regulator. In the United Kingdom, the Royal Town Planning Institute, RTPI, is the chartered professional body for planners. In the United States, AICP is a professional certification awarded by the American Institute of Certified Planners, part of the American Planning Association; it is not a government licence, and state rules vary.

sections.heading: Practice and liability
sections.text: Planners work in the public sector, in private consultancy or in both over a career. Public-sector planners prepare plans, advise councils and administer development control.
